reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: A venous aneurysm is a localised saccular or fusiform dilatation of a vein arising without an antecedent arteriovenous fistula or pseudoaneurysm; these lesions are uncommon and are often congenital or idiopathic
Popliteal venous aneurysm is the most clinically important type because it is a well-recognised source of recurrent pulmonary embolism, which may occur despite adequate anticoagulation
Presentations range from an asymptomatic popliteal swelling to leg pain, deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, and a mass that changes with posture or Valsalva is suggestive
Internal jugular venous aneurysm (phlebectasia) typically presents in children as a soft, compressible neck swelling that enlarges on straining and is usually benign
Duplex ultrasound is the principal diagnostic test, while cross-sectional venography by CT or MR delineates the anatomy for surgical planning and helps to identify intraluminal thrombus

Surgical repair, such as tangential aneurysmorrhaphy with lateral venorrhaphy or resection with an end-to-end anastomosis or interposition graft, is recommended for popliteal venous aneurysm because of the embolic risk, generally with perioperative anticoagulation
Small or superficial saccular aneurysms elsewhere may be observed with surveillance, whereas deep venous aneurysms containing thrombus or associated with embolism warrant intervention
reference.pathophysiology: Venous aneurysms arise from a focal weakness of the vein wall with loss of the normal balance of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, allowing localised dilatation. The cause is frequently congenital or idiopathic, although trauma, chronic inflammation, degenerative change and localised elevations in venous pressure are implicated. The dilated segment behaves as a low-flow reservoir in which turbulence and stasis promote the formation of mural thrombus; within a deep vein such as the popliteal, this thrombus can detach and embolise to the pulmonary circulation. A saccular morphology tends to carry a greater thrombogenic and embolic risk than a fusiform dilatation.
additionalDifferentials: Soft tissue tumour such as lipoma or sarcoma
Lymph node mass or cystic lymphangioma
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound as the first-line diagnostic study
CT or MR venography to define morphology and extent
Contrast venography where the anatomy remains unclear
CT pulmonary angiography when pulmonary embolism is suspected
Careful imaging assessment for intraluminal thrombus
Thrombophilia screen in patients presenting with thromboembolism
Comparative arterial imaging to distinguish from an arterial aneurysm when the site is ambiguous
redFlags: Pulmonary embolism, especially when recurrent or occurring despite anticoagulation
Intraluminal thrombus demonstrated within the aneurysm
Rapid enlargement or symptoms of local compression
Saccular morphology of a deep (popliteal) venous aneurysm
Rupture, though rare, or features of an acute deep vein thrombosis
reference.prognosis: Superficial and small venous aneurysms are generally benign and can be observed. Popliteal and other deep venous aneurysms carry a genuine risk of potentially fatal pulmonary embolism, but surgical repair has good long-term outcomes with a low rate of recurrence.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing a popliteal venous aneurysm as a Baker cyst and thereby missing the embolic risk
Relying on anticoagulation alone for a popliteal venous aneurysm, which does not reliably prevent recurrent embolism
Failing to image for intraluminal thrombus before planning intervention
Overlooking a venous aneurysm as the source in unexplained or recurrent pulmonary embolism
Attempting to distinguish a venous from an arterial aneurysm on clinical grounds alone
